summary.title: The 7 quests of resilient software design
summary.one_liner: Seven conceptual "quests" for designing resilient distributed systems, covering business value, non-determinism, avoiding 100% availability targets, Dev/Ops feedback loops, functional design, resilience patterns, and preserving community knowledge.
takeaways: Resilience is about not losing money, and it is limited by a resilience budget.
Distributed systems are non-deterministic, so plan to detect and recover from inconsistencies rather than assume determinism.
Avoid the 100% availability trap: availability compounds across many service calls (e.g., 99.5% across 10 services is about 95.1%).
Establish a working Dev-Ops feedback loop (DevOps or SRE) so resilience measures can be measured and improved.
Good functional design (isolation via bulkheads, short activation paths, careful reuse) matters more than any individual pattern; use patterns selectively.
summary.summary: This is a slide deck (87 slides) by Uwe Friedrichsen, CTO at codecentric, presenting seven "quests" for resilient software design through talk-style slides with diagrams and references to classic distributed systems papers. It argues that resilience is about avoiding lost revenue, that distributed systems require non-deterministic thinking, and that targeting 100% availability is a trap. It then covers Dev/Ops feedback loops, functional design for isolation (bulkheads, caching trade-offs), a catalogue of resilience patterns grouped by core, detect, treat, prevent, recover, mitigate, and complement, and how Erlang/Akka and Netflix applied them. The final quest concerns preserving the community's collective memory. The page text is slide content only, so the depth of each point is limited to what the slides state.
